tier_reason: README states '25x faster than unzip and 10x faster than tar at reading individual files (uncompressed)' and shows first-party benchmark screenshots (M1X macOS, unnamed Ubuntu AMD64 server); no benchmark script, compiler flags or server CPU model, so C.

corrections.caveats: No license file (LICENSE, LICENSE.md, LICENSE.txt all 404), so reference only. Benchmarks are screenshots only, with no script, flags or server CPU model. The author says it was written in about 3 hours with no tests and no checksums (unsafe for untrusted data), ignores symlinks, and is limited to 4 GB. HN commenters say the right baseline is an indexed archive such as asar, not tar or unzip. It is an archive format, which sits at the edge of filesystems-and-io.

notes: The 25x/10x headline is in the README text; the per-benchmark numbers are only in images, which I did not read. I could not see the last commit date (2021-11-10) on the page, so I left it unchanged. 359 stars confirmed; not a fork.

tier_reason: docs/benchmark.md has first-party tables against safetensors 0.7.0, fastsafetensors 0.2.2 and Run:ai Model Streamer 0.15.6; every claimed number matches. The README points to tests/test.py as the benchmark harness, but CPU model and compiler flags are not stated, so not A.

corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark. CPU model and compiler flags are not given, so tier C; the README names tests/test.py as the full benchmark harness. The baseline is the safetensors Python loader, not a raw POSIX read loop. On tmpfs the DeepSeek-R1 gain shrinks to 1.87x, and fastsafetensors and RMS are slower than plain safetensors there. With copy=False, list(f.tensors()) silently corrupts data when buffer_size < total_tensor_size (README warning). A repo (123123213weqw/siphon) republishes the identical table and is not reported separately.

notes: All 50 GB/s and tmpfs numbers match docs/benchmark.md exactly. Apache-2.0 LICENSE confirmed. I did not check the star count (83).

tier_reason: article.md gives min/median/max over 10 runs against Rust b3sum, cat, dd and fio, with code, gcc -O3 compile lines, Debian 12 and kernel 6.1.0-9; the CPU model is never named (only 'AMD64 with sha_ni, AVX2, no AVX512'), so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 1 GiB cold cache: 0.301s (singlethread, median) vs 0.386s b3sum --no-mmap median (min 0.381s) and 0.4105s b3sum --num-threads 1 median (0.404-0.416s); cat to /dev/null 0.302s. 10 GiB: 2.899s vs cat to /dev/null 2.904s (medians). The author says it is about 25% faster than official b3sum and at NVMe line rate (about 3533 MiB/s).
corrections.caveats: First-party blog numbers; CPU model not stated, so tier C. No license file (LICENSE 404), so reference only. The gain over cat (0.301s vs 0.302s) is within noise; the real gap is versus Rust b3sum on a cold disk. The page cache is flushed before each run, so the test is I/O-bound by design. The author reports output hashes match official b3sum.

notes: All numbers verified in article.md (table columns are min/median/max). I did not see the last commit date on the page, so I left 2023-08-02 unchanged. 3 stars confirmed.
